reasoning.Student A: The mechanism is strategy-proof, so truthful reporting is a dominant strategy: no ranking I submit can give me a better outcome than ranking schools in true order, regardless of what others do. My true preferences are w > y > z > x. I also have top priority (1) at w and y, which makes it likely I will get one of those if available. Although many others favor y > x > w > z, misrepresenting (for example, ranking y above w) cannot improve my assignment under a strategy-proof mechanism. Therefore I should and will submit my true ranking.
reasoning.Student B: Because the mechanism is strategy-proof, I cannot improve my assignment by misrepresenting preferences regardless of what others do. My true ranking is w > y > x > z. Even though many other applicants prefer y > x > w > z and my priorities are w:2, x:1, y:2, z:1, that does not change the fact that reporting anything other than my true order cannot give me a better outcome under a strategy-proof mechanism. Therefore I should and will report my true preferences.

My true ordering is w > x > y > z. Although many applicants favor y > x > w > z and my priority at y (4) is lower than at w and x (3), this does not change that truthful reporting is optimal under a strategy-proof mechanism. Therefore I will rank the schools in my true preference order.
reasoning.Student D: The mechanism is strategy-proof, so truthful reporting is a dominant strategy: no matter what other students submit, you cannot get a better assignment by misrepresenting your preferences. Given that, and given my true values (w > z > x > y), I should submit that true ranking. Although my priority at w and x is relatively low and many applicants favor y and x, misreporting cannot improve my outcome under a strategy-proof mechanism and could only make it worse.
